question: Air brakes are actually made up of three different braking systems. Which of the following correctly lists them?
choice_a: Service brake, parking brake, and emergency brake
choice_b: Primary brake, secondary brake, and auxiliary brake
choice_c: Foot brake, hand brake, and trailer brake
choice_d: Drum brake, disc brake, and spring brake
explanation: The manual states air brakes are really three different systems: the service brake applies and releases the brakes during normal driving, the parking brake applies and releases the parking brakes, and the emergency brake uses parts of the service and parking systems to stop the vehicle in a brake system failure.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-1

question: What powers the air compressor in an air brake system?
choice_a: It pumps air using an electric motor separate from the engine
choice_b: It is connected to the engine through gears or a v-belt
choice_c: It draws air directly from the brake chambers
choice_d: It is powered by the vehicle's hydraulic system
explanation: The manual explains the air compressor pumps air into the air storage tanks and is connected to the engine through gears or a v-belt; it may be air cooled or engine-coolant cooled, and may have its own oil supply or be lubricated by engine oil.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-1

question: In a typical air brake system, at approximately what pressure does the governor stop the compressor from pumping air (the "cut-out" level)?
choice_a: 80 psi
choice_b: 100 psi
choice_c: 125 psi
choice_d: 150 psi
explanation: The governor controls the compressor: when tank pressure rises to about 125 psi ("cut-out"), the governor stops the compressor from pumping; when pressure falls to about 100 psi ("cut-in"), the governor lets the compressor start pumping again.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-1

question: What is the purpose of air storage tanks (reservoirs) in an air brake system?
choice_a: To cool the compressed air before it reaches the brake chambers
choice_b: To hold compressed air so the brakes can be used several times even if the compressor stops working
choice_c: To filter oil out of the air before it reaches the compressor
choice_d: To store fuel for the engine
explanation: Air storage tanks hold compressed air and will hold enough to allow the brakes to be used several times even if the compressor stops working; the number and size of tanks varies among vehicles.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-1

question: If a vehicle's air tanks do NOT have automatic drain valves, what must the driver do?
choice_a: Drain the tanks manually at the end of each day of driving
choice_b: Drain the tanks only once a month
choice_c: Never drain the tanks, since they self-clean
choice_d: Have a mechanic drain them annually
explanation: Compressed air carries water and compressor oil that collect in the bottom of the tank; with manually operated drain valves, the driver must drain the tanks at the end of each day of driving, since water can freeze in cold weather and cause brake failure.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-1

question: What is the purpose of an alcohol evaporator on some air brake systems?
choice_a: To clean the brake linings of dust and debris
choice_b: To put alcohol into the air system to reduce the risk of ice forming in air brake valves during cold weather
choice_c: To cool the air compressor during heavy use
choice_d: To lubricate the brake pedal linkage
explanation: An alcohol evaporator puts alcohol into the air system to help reduce the risk of ice in air brake valves and other parts during cold weather, since ice inside the system can make the brakes stop working; the container should be checked and filled daily during cold weather.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-2

question: Where is the safety (relief) valve installed in an air brake system, and at what pressure is it usually set to open?
choice_a: In the brake pedal assembly, at about 55 psi
choice_b: In the first tank the air compressor pumps air to, at about 150 psi
choice_c: In the last tank before the brake chambers, at about 100 psi
choice_d: In the parking brake control valve, at about 125 psi
explanation: A safety relief valve is installed in the first tank the air compressor pumps air to and is usually set to open at 150 psi to protect the tank and system from too much pressure; if it releases air, something is wrong and a mechanic should fix the fault.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-2

question: The air brake pedal is also known by what other name(s)?
choice_a: The master cylinder
choice_b: The foot valve or treadle valve
choice_c: The modulating valve
choice_d: The wig wag valve
explanation: The manual states the brake pedal is also called the foot valve or treadle valve; pushing it down harder applies more air pressure, and releasing it lets compressed air out of the system, which must be made up by the compressor.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-2

question: In s-cam drum brakes, what happens when the driver pushes the brake pedal?
choice_a: Air is let into each brake chamber, pushing a rod that turns the s-cam and forces the brake shoes against the drum
choice_b: Hydraulic fluid is released directly into the brake drum
choice_c: A wedge is pulled out from between the brake shoes, releasing the brakes
choice_d: The power screw clamps a rotor between caliper pads
explanation: Air pressure pushes the brake chamber rod out, moving the slack adjuster and twisting the brake camshaft, which turns the s-cam so it forces the brake shoes apart and presses them against the inside of the brake drum. (Choice D describes air-operated disc brakes, not s-cam brakes.)
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-2

question: What does it mean if a driver notices they must apply increasing application pressure to hold the same speed?
choice_a: The parking brake is engaged
choice_b: The brakes are fading, and the driver should slow down and use a lower gear
choice_c: The ABS system has malfunctioned
choice_d: The air tanks are overfilled
explanation: The manual states that increasing application pressure needed to hold the same speed means the brakes are fading; the driver should slow down and use a lower gear, and the need for increased pressure can also be caused by brakes out of adjustment, air leaks, or mechanical problems.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-3

question: On a vehicle with air brakes, at what pressure must a visible low air pressure warning signal come on?
choice_a: Before pressure falls below 55 psi
choice_b: Before pressure falls below 100 psi
choice_c: Before pressure falls below 125 psi
choice_d: Before pressure falls below 20 psi
explanation: A low air pressure warning signal (usually a red light, sometimes with a buzzer) is required and must come on before the air pressure in the tanks falls below 55 psi, or one half the compressor governor cutout pressure on older vehicles.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-3

question: How does a "wig wag" low air pressure warning device work?
choice_a: It sounds a horn continuously until the engine is turned off
choice_b: It drops a mechanical arm into the driver's view when system pressure drops below 55 psi
choice_c: It automatically applies the parking brake at 100 psi
choice_d: It flashes the headlights when pressure exceeds 125 psi
explanation: A wig wag drops a mechanical arm into the driver's view when system pressure drops below 55 psi; an automatic wig wag rises out of view once pressure rises above 55 psi, while a manual reset type must be placed in the out-of-view position by hand.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-3

topic: Low Air Pressure Warning on Large Buses
question: On large buses, at what pressure range is it common for low air pressure warning devices to signal?
explanation: The manual notes that on large buses it is common for the low pressure warning devices to signal at 80-85 psi, a higher threshold than the standard 55 psi used on most other vehicles.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-3

question: What did older front brake limiting valves (found on vehicles made before 1975) do when set to the "slippery" position?
choice_a: They doubled the pressure sent to the front brakes for better stopping power
choice_b: They cut the normal air pressure to the front brakes by half
choice_c: They locked the front brakes completely
choice_d: They disconnected the front brakes entirely
explanation: In the "slippery" position, the limiting valve cut the normal air pressure to the front brakes by half; the manual notes this actually reduced the vehicle's stopping power, since tests show front wheel skids from braking are not likely even on ice, so the control should normally be left in "normal."
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-3

question: Why are spring brakes typically used for the parking and emergency brake systems on trucks, truck tractors, and buses?
choice_a: Because they must be held on by mechanical force, since air pressure can eventually leak away
choice_b: Because they use hydraulic fluid, which never leaks
choice_c: Because they only work when the engine is running
choice_d: Because they are cheaper to manufacture than air-only brakes
explanation: Parking and emergency brakes must be held on by mechanical force because air pressure can eventually leak away; spring brakes use powerful springs held back by air pressure, and removing that air lets the springs put on the brakes.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-4

question: On newer vehicles with air brakes, how does a driver apply the parking (spring) brakes using the cab control?
choice_a: By pushing in a round blue knob
choice_b: By pulling out a diamond-shaped, yellow, push-pull control knob
choice_c: By flipping a red toggle switch
choice_d: By turning a key to the "park" position
explanation: On newer vehicles, the parking brakes (spring brakes) are put on by pulling out a diamond-shaped, yellow, push-pull control knob, and released by pushing it in; on older vehicles the parking brakes may instead be controlled by a lever.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-4

question: What caution does the manual give about the brake pedal and spring brakes?
choice_a: Never push the brake pedal down when the spring brakes are on, as the combined forces could damage the brakes
choice_b: Always push the brake pedal down when the spring brakes are on, to test them
choice_c: The brake pedal is mechanically disconnected whenever spring brakes are applied
choice_d: Pushing the brake pedal while spring brakes are on has no effect on the vehicle
explanation: The manual warns that you should never push the brake pedal down when the spring brakes are on, because the brakes could be damaged by the combined forces of the springs and the air pressure; not all systems are designed to prevent this, and even those that are may not always work.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-4

question: On some vehicles, such as buses, what is the purpose of dual parking control valves with a separate air tank?
choice_a: To provide extra braking power on steep downgrades
choice_b: To let the driver temporarily release the spring brakes using a separate air supply, so the vehicle can be moved in an emergency
choice_c: To automatically drain water from the main air tanks
choice_d: To increase the low air pressure warning threshold
explanation: A separate air tank lets the driver push in a control to temporarily release the spring brakes and move the vehicle in an emergency; there is only enough air in the separate tank to do this a few times, so the driver must plan carefully.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-4

question: According to the manual, which vehicles are required to be equipped with antilock brakes (ABS)?
choice_a: Only passenger vehicles manufactured after 2000
choice_b: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997, and other air brake vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, converter dollies) built on or after March 1, 1998
choice_c: Only vehicles that tow doubles or triples
choice_d: All commercial vehicles, regardless of manufacture date
explanation: The manual states truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997, and other air brake vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, and converter dollies) built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have ABS; drivers can check the certification label for the date of manufacture.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-4

question: What color are the ABS malfunction lamps required on vehicles equipped with antilock brakes?
choice_a: Red
choice_b: Green
choice_c: Yellow
choice_d: Blue
explanation: Vehicles with ABS have yellow malfunction lamps; tractors, trucks, and buses have them on the instrument panel, while trailers have them on the left side, either the front or rear corner, and dollies made on or after March 1, 1998 are required to have one on the left side.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-4

question: In a dual air brake system, what do the "primary" and "secondary" systems typically control?
choice_a: The primary system controls the trailer brakes only; the secondary controls the tractor brakes only
choice_b: The primary system typically operates the regular brakes on the rear axle(s); the secondary operates the regular brakes on the front axle (and possibly one rear axle)
choice_c: The primary system controls parking brakes; the secondary controls service brakes
choice_d: The primary and secondary systems are identical and operate simultaneously with no separate function
explanation: A dual air brake system has two separate air brake systems that use a single set of brake controls, each with its own tanks, hoses, and lines; the primary system typically operates the regular brakes on the rear axle(s), and the secondary system operates the regular brakes on the front axle (and possibly one rear axle), with both supplying air to a trailer if one is present.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-5

question: Before driving a vehicle with a dual air brake system, what minimum pressure should the driver allow the compressor to build up in both the primary and secondary systems?
choice_a: 55 psi
choice_b: 100 psi
choice_c: 125 psi
choice_d: 150 psi
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to allow time for the air compressor to build up a minimum of 100 psi pressure in both the primary and secondary systems before driving, while watching both pressure gauges and the low air pressure warning light and buzzer.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-5

question: When inspecting slack adjusters on s-cam brakes during the walk-around inspection, what indicates that a slack adjuster probably needs adjustment?
choice_a: It moves more than about one inch where the push rod attaches to it when pulled by hand
choice_b: It feels warm to the touch
choice_c: It is painted a different color than the brake drum
choice_d: It makes no sound when tapped
explanation: With the vehicle parked on level ground, wheels chocked, and parking brakes released, the driver should pull hard on each reachable slack adjuster; if it moves more than about one inch where the push rod attaches, it probably needs adjustment. Out-of-adjustment brakes are the most common problem found in roadside inspections.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-6

question: Since what year have all vehicles been required to have automatic slack adjusters, and how should manual adjustment of them be treated?
choice_a: Since 1994; manual adjustment should only be used as a temporary measure in an emergency, since it usually does not fix the underlying problem
choice_b: Since 1994; manual adjustment is the required routine maintenance procedure
choice_c: Since 2000; automatic slack adjusters never need to be checked
choice_d: Since 1975; manual adjustment should be performed daily
explanation: All vehicles built since 1994 have automatic slack adjusters, which must still be checked even though they adjust themselves during full brake applications. Manual adjustment of an automatic adjuster should only be used as a temporary measure to correct an emergency, since it is likely to soon be back out of adjustment and can give a false sense of security.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-6

question: During the air leakage rate test with a fully-charged air system, engine off, and parking brake released, what is the maximum acceptable pressure loss for a single (non-combination) vehicle?
choice_a: Less than 1 psi in one minute
choice_b: Less than 2 psi in one minute
choice_c: Less than 5 psi in one minute
choice_d: Less than 10 psi in one minute
explanation: With a fully-charged air system (typically 125 psi), engine off, and parking brake released, the loss rate should be less than two psi in one minute for single vehicles (less than three psi in one minute for combination vehicles); a higher rate means leaks must be found and fixed before driving.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-7

topic: Rate of Air Pressure Buildup Test
question: In a dual air system, with the engine running at operating rpm, how quickly should air pressure build from 85 to 100 psi?
choice_a: Within 15 seconds
choice_b: Within 45 seconds
choice_c: Within 90 seconds
choice_d: Within 3 minutes
explanation: The manual states that in dual air systems, pressure should build from 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds at operating rpm (build-up time can be longer and still safe on vehicles with larger-than-minimum tanks, per manufacturer specifications). If buildup is too slow, pressure may drop too low during driving, requiring an emergency stop.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-7

question: What is the key difference between the "controlled braking" and "stab braking" emergency stopping methods?
choice_a: Controlled braking applies the brakes as hard as possible without locking the wheels while keeping steering movements small; stab braking applies the brakes fully, releases when the wheels lock, then reapplies fully once the wheels roll again
choice_b: Controlled braking is only used on wet roads; stab braking is only used on dry roads
choice_c: Controlled braking uses the parking brake; stab braking uses the service brake
choice_d: There is no real difference; they are two names for the same technique
explanation: With controlled braking, the driver applies the brakes as hard as possible without locking the wheels and keeps steering wheel movements small. With stab braking, the driver applies the brakes fully, releases them when the wheels lock up, and reapplies fully as soon as the wheels start rolling again, since it can take up to a second for the wheels to start rolling after release.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-8

question: What four factors make up the total stopping distance for a vehicle with air brakes?
choice_a: Perception distance, reaction distance, brake lag distance, and braking distance
choice_b: Reaction distance, braking distance, tire wear, and road grade
choice_c: Perception distance, braking distance, and two separately measured braking distance factors
choice_d: Brake lag distance, tire pressure, load weight, and reaction distance
explanation: Because air brakes have an added delay called brake lag (it takes about a half second or more for air to flow through the lines to the brakes) compared to hydraulic brakes, which work instantly, total stopping distance equals perception distance plus reaction distance plus brake lag distance plus braking distance; at 55 mph the air brake lag alone adds about 32 feet, making total stopping distance over 450 feet under good conditions.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-8

question: According to the manual, when should a driver avoid using the parking brakes?
choice_a: When the vehicle is parked on a hill
choice_b: When the brakes are very hot from a steep grade, or very wet in freezing temperatures
choice_c: When the vehicle has ABS installed
choice_d: When the vehicle is fully loaded
explanation: Using the parking brakes when they are very hot (such as after a steep grade) can damage them from the heat, and using them when very wet in freezing temperatures can cause them to freeze so the vehicle cannot move; the manual recommends wheel chocks on a level surface instead, letting hot brakes cool, or driving in a low gear to heat and dry wet brakes.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 5 - Air Brakes, p. 5-9
